name: Freshwater marsh
notes: Treeless emergent wetland on mineral soil with standing fresh water: tall stands of cattail, reed and bulrush grade into sedge tussocks, iris and sweet-grass at the margins with scattered willow/sweet-gale; drawn on the North American prairie potholes and Great Lakes marshes and the European reedbeds (Danube, Norfolk Broads).

growth.juvenile_note: Seed germinates within a day on wet mud: two tiny round cotyledons and a hair-thin stem. Grows as a slender whip with narrow lance-shaped leaves, often over 1.2 m in the first year and about 10 m by age 5; leans toward light and often forks into several trunks. Stumps and broken twigs root and sprout.
growth.source: USDA Silvics of N America vol. 2 (Pitcher & McKnight): 1.2 m first year, 9.8 m at 5, 15 m at 10, 22 m at 20, 31 m at 40 yr on good sites; seed must land within 12-24 h; first seed ~10 yr; mature at 55 yr, oldest 70-85 yr; very intolerant

fruiting.source: USDA Silvics (flowers Feb in the south to late June in the north; mainly insect-pollinated, nectar, some wind; capsules 3-6 mm split 45-60 days after pollination; ~5 million seeds/kg; cottony seed viable only days); dioecious catkins 2.5-7.5 cm

growth.source: USDA FEIS Cephalanthus occidentalis (to 6 m, flowers Jun-Sep in dense spherical heads of tiny white flowers at branch ends, fruit Sep-Oct as round clusters of nutlets, ~134,000 seeds/lb, low germination without pretreatment, sprouts after fire, increases with light); growth and lifespan estimated

growth.juvenile_note: Germinates within a day on wet mud: two tiny round cotyledons, then a downy shoot with small obovate, dull grey-green leaves (grey-hairy beneath). Branches low into a rounded, dense, many-stemmed bush; twigs downy, with raised ridges under the peeled bark. Fallen or broken stems root where they touch wet ground.
growth.source: Stace, New Flora of the British Isles, and Meikle, Willows and Poplars of GB and Ireland (BSBI) for form, 4-10 (15) m size and phenology; USDA Woody Plant Seed Manual Salix (willow seed has no dormancy and germinates within 12-24 h on wet ground (USDA Woody Plant Seed Manual Salix)); growth rate, first seed and lifespan estimated for a fast, short-lived sallow

fruiting.source: Stace and Meikle (BSBI): catkins before the leaves in Mar-Apr, males 2-3 cm with yellow anthers ('pussy willow'), females grey-green; hairy flask-shaped capsules 7-10 mm shed seed May-June; key early food for bumblebee queens and honeybees; fruit set and crop estimated

shrub.name: Swamp loosestrife

growth.juvenile_note: Seed needs a winter and germinates on wet exposed peat or mud at the water's edge; the seedling is a single soft upright shoot with lance-shaped leaves in pairs or whorls. From the second year its stems arch out over the water, root where their tips touch, and build a spreading mat of arching semi-woody stems whose submerged bases swell with white spongy tissue.
growth.source: Gleason & Cronquist, Manual of Vascular Plants of NE United States and adjacent Canada (Decodon: arching stems rooting at the tips, spongy base under water); Eckert & Barrett, studies of Decodon clonal growth in Ontario wetlands

repro.note: tristylous magenta flowers worked by bees; arching stems root at their tips and walk out over open water

shrub.source: Decodon verticillatus, swamp loosestrife or water willow (Lythraceae), Kew POWO accepted, the only species of its genus; Nova Scotia and Ontario to Florida and Louisiana, west to Minnesota, in marsh margins, bog moats and shallow water, common in the Great Lakes marshes; arching semi-woody stems 1-2.5 m that root at their tips, spongy white bark under water, magenta flowers in the leaf axils. Mike listed it twice ('water willow' and 'swamp loosestrife') — Gleason & Cronquist; USDA Plants.

bark.notes: brown semi-woody stems; submerged bases swollen with thick spongy white tissue

shrub.name: Alder buckthorn

growth.juvenile_note: Seed dropped by birds germinates the next spring in wet carr and reedbed edges; the seedling is a slender whip with glossy oval, untoothed leaves and parallel veins. It branches low into a loose, open shrub of grey-brown stems; cut stems sprout.
growth.source: Biological Flora of the British Isles (Godwin 1943, Frangula alnus); USDA Woody Plant Seed Manual (Frangula: cold stratification, epigeal)

repro.note: small greenish flowers over a long season, visited by bees and wasps; berries green to red to black on the same branch; foodplant of the brimstone butterfly

shrub.source: Frangula alnus, alder buckthorn (Rhamnaceae), Kew POWO accepted; Europe to western Siberia and North Africa, in fen carr, reedbed margins and wet heath, a typical shrub of the Norfolk Broads carr and the Danube floodplain marshes; introduced and invasive in North America, so it stands for the European half of this biome only; 3-6 m — Flora Europaea; Biological Flora of the British Isles (Godwin 1943).

growth.juvenile_note: Germinates on wet mud or in shallow water: a hair-like shoot, then 2-4 tiny leaves and 2-6 ribbon leaves floating flat on the water before stiff, erect, flat grey-green leaves rise. By the end of its first summer a seedling is 60-85 cm tall and has sent rhizomes out into a clump up to 3 m across. Each shoot lives about a year; the clone persists for decades.
growth.source: USDA FEIS (Typha latifolia): germinates best at 25-30 C in high light; 2-4 small then 2-6 floating leaves before erect ones; seedlings 60-85 cm after 84 d; flowers early in 2nd year; ramets die within a year, rhizomes live about 2 yr; one seedling's rhizomes spread 3 m in a season; shade intolerant.

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings are small, weak, grass-like tufts of soft green leaves on wet mud. After a season rhizomes and long surface runners spread out; every spring new culms shoot up like thin canes to full height in a few months, with long, broad, grey-green leaves all along the stem and a big, silky, purple-brown plume that fades to grey-buff.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Phragmites australis (germination needs light, moisture and warm alternating temperatures after cold stratification; seedling survival very low; 3-4 years to viable seed; maximum height at 5-8 years; no part of a clone lives more than 8 years though clones persist far longer; culms die back yearly)

growth.juvenile_note: A small tuft of narrow leaves; the clump thickens each year from short rhizomes, and old leaf bases, roots and trapped sediment build a raised pedestal. Over years to decades this becomes a tall tussock like a pillar standing above seasonal flood water, crowned by a fountain of arching leaves.

ground.name: Mosquito fern

growth.juvenile_note: A tiny floating sporophyte: a pinhead of overlapping two-lobed scale leaves with hair-fine dangling roots, rising from a sunken megaspore or, far more often, a fragment breaking off an older plant. In days it branches into a 1-2 cm feathery triangle of bluish-green scales that blush red in strong sun and cold, soon locking with others into a velvety floating mat.
growth.source: Wikipedia (plants 1-2 cm, branch and fragment freely, cover lakes within months, die back in winter and survive as submerged buds); Azolla literature (Lumpkin & Plucknett 1980) for doubling times of ~2-5 days and late-summer sporocarps; megaspore-to-sporophyte time estimated.

repro.note: spores by wind and water; no flowers; needs a wet film to reproduce, so spread reads moisture not pollinators

ground.source: Still fresh water worldwide; floating red-green mats that carpet a pond in weeks; fixes nitrogen. Kew POWO.
